lessons.title: Can You Step into the Same River Twice?
lessons.title_zh: 人能踏進同一條河兩次嗎？
lessons.blurb_en: Heraclitus held that everything flows. Parmenides proved that nothing can change. Nearly all later metaphysics is an attempt to keep what each of them saw.
lessons.blurb_zh: 赫拉克利特主張萬物流轉。巴門尼德證明沒有東西能改變。後來幾乎全部的形上學，都是想把他們各自看到的東西同時保住。
lessons.big_en: Change needs something that persists through it, and persistence shows itself only through change. A river is the plainest case: it is the same river because its water is always different.
lessons.big_zh: 變化需要有個東西在變化之中持續下去，而持續只有透過變化才顯現出來。河是最明白的例子：它之所以是同一條河，正因為它的水總是不同的。

paras.en: Around 500 BCE, at opposite ends of the Greek world, two thinkers reached conclusions that could hardly be further apart. Heraclitus of Ephesus, on the coast of what is now Turkey, taught that the world is a process, like a fire or a river, in which nothing stays as it is. Parmenides of Elea, in southern Italy, argued that change is impossible and that what truly exists is one, whole, and motionless. Neither could be dismissed. Heraclitus had the evidence of the senses on his side, and Parmenides had an argument that nobody could answer. Philosophy after them had to explain how both could be so persuasive.
paras.zh: 大約西元前 500 年，在希臘世界的兩端，有兩位思想家得出了相距不能更遠的結論。以弗所（在今天土耳其的海岸）的赫拉克利特教導：世界是一個過程，像火或河，其中沒有任何東西保持原樣。義大利南部埃利亞的巴門尼德則論證：變化是不可能的，真正存在的東西是唯一、完整、不動的。兩個人都沒辦法被打發掉。赫拉克利特有感官的證據站在他這邊；巴門尼德有一個沒有人答得了的論證。在他們之後的哲學，必須解釋這兩者怎麼都能這麼有說服力。

paras.en: Heraclitus wrote in short, dense sayings, of which about a hundred and thirty survive as quotations in later authors. The most famous concern a river. “You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.” And, more strangely: “We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not.” Plato reported the doctrine in the form that became proverbial, that “all things are in motion and nothing at rest,” and that “you cannot go into the same water twice.”
paras.zh: 赫拉克利特用簡短而濃縮的格言寫作，其中大約一百三十條，以被後世作者引用的形式保存了下來。最有名的幾條談的是河。「你不能兩次踏進同一條河；因為新的水不斷地流到你身上。」還有更奇怪的一條：「我們踏進又沒有踏進同一條河；我們存在又不存在。」柏拉圖轉述這個學說，用的是後來成為諺語的形式：「萬物都在運動，沒有東西靜止」，以及「你不能兩次走進同樣的水」。

paras.en: It is easy to hear this as a denial that anything is ever the same, and one of his followers took it that way. Cratylus, according to Aristotle, criticized his master for saying that one cannot step twice into the same river, “for he thought one could not do it even once,” and in the end he gave up speaking and only moved his finger. But look at the first saying again. It speaks of the same rivers. Heraclitus does not deny that there is one river, the Cayster, into which the Ephesians stepped every day. His point is about what makes it one. Dam it, so that the water stops being replaced, and you no longer have a river. The sameness of the river consists in the exchange of its waters.
paras.zh: 人很容易把這聽成是在否認任何東西曾經保持同一，而他的一位追隨者就是這樣理解的。照亞里斯多德的說法，克拉底魯批評老師說「人不能兩次踏進同一條河」，「因為他認為連一次都不行」；到最後他不再說話，只動動手指。但是再看一次第一句格言。它說的是「同一條河」。赫拉克利特並不否認有一條河，凱斯特河，以弗所人天天踏進去的那一條。他的重點在於：是什麼使它成為一條河？把它攔起來，讓水不再更替，你就不再有一條河了。河的同一，就在於它的水的更替。

paras.en: Heraclitus therefore taught more than flux. He taught that the flux is ordered. The world is “an ever-living Fire, with measures of it kindling, and measures going out,” and the word to notice is “measures.” Fire is his image for a thing that exists only by consuming and being fed, and a steady flame is a balance between the two. He called the principle of this balance the logos, a word that means both “account” and “proportion,” and he complained that people live as though they each had a private understanding when the logos is common to all. He saw the same balance in opposites. “The way up and the way down is one and the same.” Day and night, waking and sleeping, the bow’s wood pulling one way and its string the other: in each case two contrary things turn out to be one process seen from two sides. “The hidden attunement,” he said, “is better than the open.”
paras.zh: 所以赫拉克利特教的不只是流變。他教的是：流變是有秩序的。世界是「一團永恆的活火，按一定的分寸燃燒，按一定的分寸熄滅」，要注意的詞是「分寸」。火是他用來比喻這樣一種東西的意象：它只有靠消耗與被餵養才存在；而穩定的火焰，是這兩者之間的平衡。他把這個平衡的原理稱為 logos，這個詞兼有「說明」與「比例」的意思；他抱怨說，人們活得好像各自有一套私人的理解，而 logos 其實是眾人共有的。他在對立的事物裡看到同樣的平衡。「上坡的路與下坡的路，是同一條路。」日與夜、醒與睡、弓的木頭往一邊拉而弦往另一邊拉：在每一種情形裡，兩個相反的東西，結果是同一個過程從兩面看過去的樣子。他說：「隱藏的和諧，勝過顯明的和諧。」

paras.en: Parmenides set out his view in a poem, in which a goddess reveals to him “the only two ways of search that can be thought of.” The first is “that It is, and that it is impossible for it not to be.” The second is “that It is not.” The second way, she says, cannot be followed at all: “For thou canst not know what is not—that is impossible—nor utter it; for it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be.” To think is to think of something. What is not, is nothing, and nothing is not there to be thought of.
paras.zh: 巴門尼德用一首詩陳述他的看法；詩中有一位女神向他揭示「僅有的兩條可以設想的探究之路」。第一條是：「它存在，而且它不可能不存在。」第二條是：「它不存在。」女神說，第二條路根本走不通：「因為你無法認識不存在的東西——那是不可能的——也無法說出它；因為能被思想的與能存在的，是同一回事。」思想，就是思想到某個東西。不存在的就是無，而無並不在那裡供人思想。

paras.en: From this the rest follows with terrible ease. For a thing to come into being, it would have to come from what is not, and there is no such thing. For a thing to change, it would have to become what it is not. For there to be two things, there would have to be something between them that is not either of them. So what is “is uncreated and indestructible,” single, continuous, and unmoving. The changing world of the senses is an appearance that mortals have agreed to name. Parmenides’ pupil Zeno wrote the paradoxes of lesson A4 in order to show that those who laughed at this conclusion were worse off than his master.
paras.zh: 由此，其餘的一切輕易得可怕地推了出來。一樣東西要生成，就得從不存在的東西而來，而沒有這樣的東西。一樣東西要改變，就得變成它所不是的。要有兩樣東西，它們之間就得有某個既不是這個、也不是那個的東西。所以存在者是「不生不滅的」，唯一、連續、不動。感官所見的那個變動的世界，是凡人約定命名出來的表象。巴門尼德的學生芝諾，寫下了 A4 那一課的悖論，為的是證明：嘲笑這個結論的人，處境比他的老師更糟。

paras.en: The next two centuries of Greek philosophy can be read as a series of attempts to grant Parmenides his premise and still keep the river. The atomists accepted that what truly exists never comes into being or perishes, and said that there are countless such things, atoms, whose rearrangement in empty space is what we call change. Plato divided the world in two. The Forms are as Parmenides described, eternal and unchanging, and they are what knowledge is about. The world we perceive is as Heraclitus described, and of it we have only opinion.
paras.zh: 此後兩個世紀的希臘哲學，可以讀成一連串的嘗試：承認巴門尼德的前提，同時還把那條河保住。原子論者接受「真正存在的東西既不生成也不毀滅」，然後說：這樣的東西有無數個，就是原子；它們在虛空裡的重新排列，就是我們所說的變化。柏拉圖把世界一分為二。理型正如巴門尼德所描述的，永恆而不變，是知識的對象。我們感知的世界正如赫拉克利特所描述的，對它我們只有意見。

paras.en: Aristotle’s answer has lasted longest. He pointed out that “is not” is ambiguous. An acorn is not an oak, but it is not simply nothing either. It is potentially an oak. Change is the passage from being something potentially to being it actually, and it always has three terms: something that persists, a condition it lacked, and a condition it acquires. When a green leaf turns red, the leaf remains. Change, on this analysis, requires sameness. Parmenides was right that nothing comes from nothing, and wrong to think that change needs it to.
paras.zh: 亞里斯多德的答案流傳得最久。他指出，「不是」是有歧義的。一顆橡實不是橡樹，但它也不是單純的「無」；它「潛在地」是一棵橡樹。變化，就是從「潛在地是某物」過渡到「現實地是某物」；它永遠有三項：一個持續存在的東西、一個它原本缺少的狀態、一個它後來獲得的狀態。綠葉變紅，葉子還在。照這個分析，變化需要同一。巴門尼德說「無中不能生有」是對的；他以為變化需要「無中生有」，那就錯了。

paras.en: At about the time Heraclitus was writing, Confucius stood beside a river and said: “What passes away is like this, is it not? It does not cease, day or night” (逝者如斯夫，不舍晝夜). The Analects gives no explanation, and readers have supplied two. One hears a sigh over time and mortality, the feeling that everything is carried off. The other, which became standard among the Neo-Confucians, hears admiration. The stream never rests, and the person who is learning should be like it. Both readings find in the river what Heraclitus found there. Heraclitus made a theory of the world from it, and the Chinese tradition took it as a lesson in how to live.
paras.zh: 大約在赫拉克利特寫作的同時，孔子站在一條河邊說：「逝者如斯夫！不舍晝夜。」《論語》沒有給任何解釋，讀者補上了兩種。一種聽到的是對時間與生命有限的嘆息，覺得一切都被帶走了。另一種，後來成為宋明理學家的標準讀法，聽到的是讚嘆：這條水流從不停歇，求學的人應當像它。兩種讀法在河裡找到的，都是赫拉克利特在那裡找到的東西。赫拉克利特從它造出一套關於世界的理論，中國的傳統則把它當作一堂怎麼活的課。

paras.en: Neither side has gone away. Modern physics has a Parmenidean face. Its deepest laws are conservation laws, statements that some quantity stays the same through every change, and the theory of relativity is often read as describing a four-dimensional “block” in which past, present, and future are equally real and nothing flows at all. It also has a Heraclitean face. A flame, a whirlpool, a living cell, and a human body are stable patterns in a stream of matter and energy, and they exist only as long as the stream continues. If you take the first picture as basic you have to explain why we seem to experience change. If you take the second as basic you have to explain what it is that stays the same. The river is where the two questions meet, and that is why the saying is still quoted after twenty-five centuries.
paras.zh: 兩邊都沒有消失。現代物理學有一張巴門尼德的臉。它最深的定律是守恆定律，也就是「某個量在一切變化中保持不變」的陳述；而相對論常被解讀為在描述一個四維的「塊體」，其中過去、現在、未來同樣真實，根本沒有任何東西在流動。它也有一張赫拉克利特的臉。火焰、漩渦、活細胞、人的身體，都是物質與能量之流裡的穩定樣式，只有在那道流持續的時候才存在。如果你把第一幅圖像當作根本，你就得解釋我們為什麼似乎經驗到變化。如果你把第二幅當作根本，你就得解釋保持同一的到底是什麼。河，就是這兩個問題相遇的地方；這就是為什麼這句話在兩千五百年後還在被引用。

lab.title_en: Try it: step into the river
lab.title_zh: 親手做一次：踏進這條河
lab.lead_en: A river, seen from above. Step in, and the water that touches you is marked. Watch where it goes. Then step in again, and after that stop the river and see what is left of it.
lab.lead_zh: 一條河，從上方看。踏進去，碰到你的水會被標記起來。看它去了哪裡。然後再踏進去一次；之後把河停下來，看它還剩下什麼。

start.en: The river flows past a rock. Press “Step in.”
start.zh: 河水流過一塊石頭。按「踏進去」。

step1.en: The orange drops are the water that touched your foot. Count how many are still near you.
step1.zh: 橘色的水滴，是碰到你腳的那些水。數數看還有幾滴在你附近。

gone.en: None of the water you stepped into is still here. The banks, the rock, and the eddy behind it have not moved.
gone.zh: 你踏進去的那些水，已經一滴都不在這裡了。河岸、石頭、石頭後面的漩渦，都沒有動。

step2.en: You have stepped in again. The blue-green drops are new: not one of them was here the first time. Heraclitus: “fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you.”
step2.zh: 你又踏進去了一次。青綠色的水滴是新的：第一次的時候，它們沒有一滴在這裡。赫拉克利特：「新的水不斷地流到你身上。」

frozen.en: The river is stopped. Now the water really is the same from one moment to the next, and what you are looking at is no longer a river. Its sameness lay in the flowing.
frozen.zh: 河被停住了。現在，水從這一刻到下一刻真的是同樣的水了；而你看著的東西，已經不再是一條河。它的同一，原來就在流動裡。

pattern.en: The eddy behind the rock keeps its shape and its place while every drop in it is replaced. It is a pattern in the water. You are something like this yourself.
pattern.zh: 石頭後面的漩渦保持著它的形狀與位置，而其中的每一滴水都在被替換。它是水裡的一個樣式。你自己也有點像這樣。

q.en: You stepped in twice. Was it the same river?
q.zh: 你踏進去了兩次。那是同一條河嗎？

t.en: Yes. Same river, different water.
t.zh: 是。同一條河，不同的水。

opts.tag: Heraclitus, read carefully · 仔細讀的赫拉克利特

r.en: This is probably what Heraclitus meant, and Aristotle would add that the river is the form and the water is its matter. You now owe an account of what the form of a river is, when its course, its depth, and even its name can change over the centuries.
r.zh: 這大概就是赫拉克利特的意思；亞里斯多德還會補一句：河是形式，水是它的質料。現在你欠一個說明：河的「形式」是什麼？它的河道、深度，甚至它的名字，幾百年下來都可以改變。

t.en: No. Nothing was the same, so there was no “again.”
t.zh: 不是。沒有任何東西是同樣的，所以沒有「再一次」。

r.en: Then you did not step in even once, since the river changed while your foot was going down, and you are not the person who began reading this sentence. Cratylus drew the conclusion and stopped talking, because words assume that things stay put long enough to be named. If you are still willing to speak, you do not hold this view.
r.zh: 那麼你連一次都沒有踏進去，因為你的腳往下踩的時候，河就已經變了；而你也不是開始讀這個句子的那個人。克拉底魯得出了這個結論，然後不再說話，因為語言預設了事物會停留得夠久、久到可以被命名。如果你還願意開口說話，你就不持這個看法。

t.en: The question is confused. Change is not real.
t.zh: 這個問題本身就亂了。變化不是真實的。

r.en: You hold that the flowing is an appearance and that reality is one and unchanging. You have a strong argument and a hard task: to explain how a changeless reality gives rise to the appearance of change, when the appearing is itself something that happens.
r.zh: 你主張流動是表象，而實在是唯一而不變的。你有一個很強的論證，也有一項艱難的任務：解釋一個不變的實在，怎麼會產生「變化」的表象；因為「顯現」本身，就是一件發生的事。

t.en: “Same river” is only a way of speaking.
t.zh: 「同一條河」只是一種說法。

r.en: This is the answer you may have given for the ship. It works well for rivers, whose boundaries we plainly draw ourselves. The Buddhist tradition accepts it and adds that the usefulness of the way of speaking is real even though no single thing answers to the name.
r.zh: 這也許就是你對那艘船給的答案。它用在河上很合適，因為河的邊界明明是我們自己畫的。佛教傳統接受這個答案，並且補充說：雖然沒有一個單獨的東西與這個名字對應，這種說法的用處卻是真實的。

argument.lead_en: Parmenides’ argument is the first sustained deductive argument in Western philosophy, and its conclusion is that the world as we know it does not exist. Click a step to see what can be said against it.
argument.lead_zh: 巴門尼德的論證是西方哲學裡第一個一氣呵成的演繹論證，而它的結論是：我們所認識的這個世界並不存在。點任何一步，看看別人可以怎麼反對它。

steps.en: What is not cannot be thought of or spoken of, because there is nothing there to think or speak about.
steps.zh: 不存在的東西不能被思想，也不能被說出，因為那裡沒有東西可以被思想或被說。
steps.ob_en: This is the step most often attacked. Plato argued in the Sophist that “is not” usually means “is different from.” To say that the leaf is not red is to speak about the leaf, which exists, and to say that it differs from red things. Negative statements do not require a thing called Nothing.
steps.ob_zh: 這是最常被攻擊的一步。柏拉圖在《智者篇》裡論證，「不是」通常的意思是「不同於」。說「這片葉子不是紅的」，是在談這片葉子，而它是存在的；說的是它不同於紅的東西。否定的陳述，並不需要有一個叫作「無」的東西。

steps.en: For anything to come into being or to change, something that was not would have to come to be.
steps.zh: 任何東西要生成或改變，就得有某個原本不存在的東西變成存在。
steps.ob_en: Aristotle attacked here. What changes does not come from nothing. It comes from something that already exists and is potentially what it will become, as bronze is potentially a statue.
steps.ob_zh: 亞里斯多德攻擊的是這裡。變化的東西不是從「無」而來的。它來自某個已經存在、而且「潛在地」是它將要成為的東西，就像青銅潛在地是一尊雕像。

steps.en: So coming into being, perishing, and change cannot be coherently thought.
steps.zh: 所以，生成、毀滅與變化，都無法被前後一致地思想。
steps.ob_en: Follows from the first two premises. Anyone who wants to block the conclusion must reject one of them.
steps.ob_zh: 由前兩個前提推出。想擋住結論的人，必須否定其中之一。

steps.en: What cannot be coherently thought cannot be: “it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be.”
steps.zh: 不能被前後一致地思想的東西，就不能存在：「能被思想的與能存在的，是同一回事。」
steps.ob_en: A bold principle, that the limits of thought are the limits of reality. An empiricist replies that we should trust our observation of change over an argument that it is inconceivable, and conclude that we have misdescribed what we conceive.
steps.ob_zh: 一個大膽的原則：思想的界限就是實在的界限。經驗主義者回答說：比起一個說變化「不可設想」的論證，我們更應該信任自己對變化的觀察，並且推斷是我們把自己所設想的東西描述錯了。

steps.en: Therefore there is no change. What is, is one, ungenerated, and unchanging.
steps.zh: 所以，沒有變化。存在者是唯一的、不生的、不變的。
steps.ob_en: Almost nobody has accepted this conclusion, and almost everybody has learned from the argument. Its lasting gift is the demand that any account of change must say what persists.
steps.ob_zh: 幾乎沒有人接受這個結論，而幾乎每個人都從這個論證學到了東西。它留下的持久贈禮是這個要求：任何對變化的說明，都必須說出是什麼在持續。

source.work: Heraclitus and Parmenides, fragments
source.work_zh: 赫拉克利特與巴門尼德的殘篇
source.tr: translated by John Burnet, Early Greek Philosophy (public domain)
source.lead_en: Neither man’s book survives. We have only the lines that later writers happened to quote, and scholars still dispute their order and sometimes their wording.
source.lead_zh: 這兩個人的書都沒有流傳下來。我們有的只是後世作者碰巧引用的那些句子；它們的次序，有時連措辭，學者至今仍有爭論。

passages.en: You cannot step twice into the same rivers; for fresh waters are ever flowing in upon you. … We step and do not step into the same rivers; we are and are not.
passages.zh: 你不能兩次踏進同一條河；因為新的水不斷地流到你身上。……我們踏進又沒有踏進同一條河；我們存在又不存在。
passages.note_en: The second saying shows his method. He states a contradiction and leaves the reader to resolve it. We step into the same river in respect of its course and do not in respect of its water. “We are and are not” then applies the thought to ourselves, the same person and not the same stuff. Aristotle accused him of denying the law of non-contradiction. A fairer reading is that he wanted us to notice in what respect each half is true.
passages.note_zh: 第二句格言顯示了他的方法。他陳述一個矛盾，然後留給讀者自己去化解。就河道而言，我們踏進的是同一條河；就水而言，不是。接著「我們存在又不存在」把這個想法用在我們自己身上：是同一個人，卻不是同樣的材料。亞里斯多德指控他否定了不矛盾律。比較公允的讀法是：他要我們留意，每一半各自是在哪一方面為真。

passages.ref: Parmenides, fragments 4 and 5 in Burnet’s numbering
passages.en: For thou canst not know what is not—that is impossible—nor utter it; for it is the same thing that can be thought and that can be.
passages.zh: 因為你無法認識不存在的東西——那是不可能的——也無法說出它；因為能被思想的與能存在的，是同一回事。
passages.note_en: The whole system grows from this sentence. Notice the three verbs: know, utter, think. Parmenides is the first philosopher to argue from what can be said and thought to what can exist, a move that Descartes, Kant, and Wittgenstein would each make again in a different form. The speaker is a goddess, and the poem is written in the meter of Homer. He gives his argument the authority of a revelation, and it is still an argument, which the reader is told to judge by reason. (“Thou canst” is the old form of “you can.”)
passages.note_zh: 整個體系都是從這個句子長出來的。注意那三個動詞：認識、說出、思想。巴門尼德是第一位「從什麼能被說、能被想，推到什麼能存在」的哲學家；這一步，笛卡兒、康德、維根斯坦後來各自用不同的形式又走了一次。說話的是一位女神，而這首詩用的是荷馬史詩的格律。他給了自己的論證「啟示」的權威，而它仍然是一個論證，並且女神要讀者用理性去判斷它。（thou canst 是 you can 的古體。）

items.o_en: If everything is always changing, nothing can be known or even named. By the time you have said “river,” it is something else.
items.o_zh: 如果一切都一直在變，就沒有東西能被認識，甚至沒有東西能被命名。等你說出「河」這個字，它已經是別的東西了。
items.r_en: This is Plato’s objection, and it is fatal to the extreme flux of Cratylus. It does not touch Heraclitus as read above, for whom the pattern of change is constant. What we know about a river is how it flows, and what a physicist knows about a flame is the law of its burning. Science is largely the search for what stays fixed in what changes.
items.r_zh: 這是柏拉圖的反駁；對克拉底魯那種極端的流變說，它是致命的。但它碰不到上面那樣解讀的赫拉克利特，因為對他來說，變化的樣式是恆定的。我們對一條河的了解，是它怎麼流；物理學家對一團火焰的了解，是它燃燒的法則。科學大體上就是在變動的東西裡，尋找固定不變的東西。

items.o_en: Parmenides is refuted every time someone crosses a room. An argument against a plain fact must contain a mistake, and there is no need to find it.
items.o_zh: 每當有人走過一個房間，巴門尼德就被駁倒了一次。一個反對明顯事實的論證，裡面一定有錯，而我們不需要把它找出來。
items.r_en: The first sentence is true, and the second is a refusal to do philosophy. Parmenides knew that people cross rooms. His claim was that our description of what happens when they do is incoherent. The replies of Plato and Aristotle took the argument seriously enough to find the fault in it, and logic and the theory of change are what they got for their trouble.
items.r_zh: 第一句話是真的；第二句話是拒絕做哲學。巴門尼德知道人會走過房間。他的主張是：我們對「人走過房間時發生了什麼」的描述，是前後不一致的。柏拉圖與亞里斯多德的回應，把這個論證看得夠認真，認真到去找出它的毛病；邏輯學與變化的理論，就是他們費這番工夫的收穫。

items.o_en: Heraclitus says that opposites are the same. That is a plain contradiction, and from a contradiction anything follows.
items.o_zh: 赫拉克利特說對立的東西是同一的。那是明明白白的矛盾；而從矛盾可以推出任何東西。
items.r_en: He says that the way up and the way down are one, which is true of any road. His examples are of a single thing that has contrary descriptions from different standpoints or at different times: sea water is healthy for fish and deadly for men. That is no contradiction. The serious question is whether he meant more than this, and some of his sayings suggest that he did.
items.r_zh: 他說的是上坡的路與下坡的路是同一條，而這對任何一條路都是真的。他舉的例子，都是同一個東西從不同的立場、或在不同的時間，有相反的描述：海水對魚有益，對人致命。這並不矛盾。認真的問題是：他的意思是不是不止於此？他的某些格言暗示，是的。

said.claim: “You cannot step into the same river twice.” (Heraclitus)
said.claim_zh: 「人不能兩次踏進同一條河。」（赫拉克利特）
said.en: The sentence in this form comes from Plato’s Cratylus, where it is introduced with the words “Heracleitus is supposed to say.” Many scholars think that the nearest thing to Heraclitus’s own words is a different fragment: on those who step into the same rivers, different and again different waters flow. That sentence asserts that the rivers are the same. If the scholars are right, the most famous line in early Greek philosophy reverses its author’s meaning.
said.zh: 這個形式的句子出自柏拉圖的《克拉底魯篇》，而且是用「據說赫拉克利特說過」這幾個字引出來的。許多學者認為，最接近赫拉克利特本人用語的是另一條殘篇：對那些踏進同一條河的人，流過來的是不同的、又不同的水。那個句子主張的是：河是同一條。如果這些學者是對的，那麼早期希臘哲學裡最有名的一句話，把作者的意思顛倒了。

terms.d_en: Continuous change; the doctrine that all things are in process.
terms.d_zh: 持續不斷的變化；主張萬物都在過程之中的學說。

terms.d_en: In Heraclitus, the rational principle or measure that governs change.
terms.d_zh: 在赫拉克利特，指支配變化的理性原則或分寸。

terms.d_en: The doctrine that contrary things are aspects of one process.
terms.d_zh: 主張相反的事物是同一個過程的不同面向。

terms.d_en: What simply is, as against what comes to be and passes away.
terms.d_zh: 單純「是」的東西，相對於生成與消逝的東西。

terms.d_en: The view that reality is one thing, or of one kind.
terms.d_zh: 主張實在是一個東西，或只有一種。

terms.d_en: Aristotle’s pair of concepts for analyzing change: what a thing can become, and what it is.
terms.d_zh: 亞里斯多德用來分析變化的一對概念：一樣東西能夠成為什麼，以及它現在是什麼。

terms.d_en: The thing that persists, and the features it gains and loses.
terms.d_zh: 持續存在的那個東西，以及它獲得與失去的特徵。

terms.d_en: The modern view, associated with A. N. Whitehead, that events and processes are more basic than things.
terms.d_zh: 現代的一種看法，與懷海德有關：事件與歷程比事物更基本。

vocab.eg: Neither thinker could be dismissed.
vocab.eg_zh: 兩位思想家都沒辦法被打發掉。

vocab.eg: Heraclitus wrote in short, dense sayings.
vocab.eg_zh: 赫拉克利特用簡短而濃縮的格言寫作。

vocab.zh: 成為諺語的、眾所周知的
vocab.eg: Plato reported the doctrine in the form that became proverbial.
vocab.eg_zh: 柏拉圖轉述這個學說，用的是後來成為諺語的形式。

vocab.eg: The sameness of the river consists in the exchange of its waters.
vocab.eg_zh: 河的同一，就在於它的水的更替。

vocab.eg: From this the rest follows with terrible ease.
vocab.eg_zh: 由此，其餘的一切輕易得可怕地推了出來。

vocab.eg: Those who laughed at the conclusion were worse off than his master.
vocab.eg_zh: 嘲笑這個結論的人，處境比他的老師更糟。

vocab.eg: They tried to grant Parmenides his premise and still keep the river.
vocab.eg_zh: 他們試著承認巴門尼德的前提，同時還把河保住。

vocab.eg: Aristotle pointed out that “is not” is ambiguous.
vocab.eg_zh: 亞里斯多德指出，「不是」是有歧義的。

vocab.eg: One hears the feeling that everything is carried off.
vocab.eg_zh: 有人聽到的是「一切都被帶走了」的感受。

vocab.eg: If you take the first picture as basic, you have to explain why we seem to experience change.
vocab.eg_zh: 如果你把第一幅圖像當作根本，就得解釋我們為什麼似乎經驗到變化。

quiz.q: On the reading given in the essay, what makes a river the same river?
options: The continual exchange of its waters within a constant pattern.
The fact that its water never changes.
Its name alone.
Nothing; there are no rivers.

quiz.q: What does Heraclitus mean by the logos?
options: The measure or law that governs change.
A god who created the world.
The art of public speaking.
The first element, water.

quiz.q: Why, according to Parmenides, is change impossible?
options: It would require something to come from what is not, and what is not cannot even be thought.
The senses show that nothing moves.
The gods forbid it.
Time has not yet begun.

quiz.q: How does Aristotle answer Parmenides?
options: Change is from being something potentially to being it actually, with something persisting throughout.
He agrees that change is unreal.
He says that atoms rearrange in the void.
He denies that anything exists.

quiz.q: What are the two traditional readings of Confucius’s words on the riverbank?
options: A sigh over passing time, and praise of ceaseless effort.
A complaint about floods, and a prayer for rain.
A joke, and a riddle.
A geography lesson, and a poem about fishing.

write.en: Name something in your life that has stayed the same only by continually changing: a friendship, a language, a school. What is the “water,” and what is the “river”?
write.zh: 舉出你生活裡一樣「只有靠不斷改變才保持同一」的東西：一段友誼、一種語言、一所學校。什麼是它的「水」？什麼是它的「河」？

write.en: Which reading of “逝者如斯夫” do you prefer, the sigh or the encouragement? Translate the line into English in your own words and defend your choice in about 100 words.
write.zh: 「逝者如斯夫」的兩種讀法，嘆息與勉勵，你偏好哪一種？用你自己的話把這句譯成英文，並用大約 100 個英文字為你的選擇辯護。

write.en: Explain to a friend why Parmenides’ argument is hard to answer, even though its conclusion is plainly false.
write.zh: 向朋友解釋：巴門尼德的論證為什麼很難回答，儘管它的結論明顯是假的。

paras.en: On impermanence the Buddha and Heraclitus say nearly the same thing, and they use the same image. “All conditioned things are impermanent” (sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā), says the Dhammapada. A discourse in the Aṅguttara Nikāya compares human life to a mountain river, flowing far and fast, of which there is no moment, no instant, no second when it turns back (7.74). Later Buddhist philosophers took the thought to its limit and held that each thing lasts only a moment, so that what we call one object is a rapid series of similar ones. That is very close to the position of Cratylus.
paras.zh: 在無常這件事上，佛陀與赫拉克利特說的幾乎一樣，而且用了同一個意象。《法句經》說：「一切行無常」（sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā）。《增支部》有一部經把人的生命比作山間的河流，流得遠、流得急，沒有一剎那、一瞬間、一須臾是會回頭的（7.74）。後來的佛教哲學家把這個想法推到極限，主張每一樣東西只存續一剎那，所以我們稱為「一個物體」的，是一連串快速相續的相似者。這跟克拉底魯的立場非常接近。

paras.en: The differences are instructive. Heraclitus’s flux has something permanent in it. The logos does not change, and the fire is ever-living. Early Buddhism names no such underlying stuff, and its regularity, dependent origination, is a pattern among events and is not treated as a thing in its own right. The two also disagree about what the insight is for. To Heraclitus the fire of the world is something to be understood and admired. In the Fire Sermon the Buddha tells his monks that “all is burning,” the eye, the ear, the mind, burning with greed, hatred, and delusion, and the point of seeing this is to let the fire go out (Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.28). The word nirvāṇa means exactly that. And where the Greek debate had two sides, the Buddhist tradition counts three. Against Parmenides it denies that anything is permanent. Against the extreme of Cratylus it affirms that conditions reliably give rise to their effects. Its own position is the middle one, that there is continuity and no identity (Dharma and the West, D5).
paras.zh: 差別之處很有啟發性。赫拉克利特的流變裡，有某種恆常的東西：logos 不變，那團火是「永恆的活火」。早期佛教沒有指認任何這樣的底層材料；它的規律性——緣起——是事件之間的一種樣式，沒有被當成一個獨立自存的東西。兩者對於「這個洞見是拿來做什麼的」也看法不同。對赫拉克利特來說，世界之火是要被理解、被讚嘆的。在〈燃燒經〉裡，佛陀告訴比丘們「一切都在燃燒」：眼、耳、意，被貪、瞋、癡之火燃燒；而看見這一點，是為了讓火熄滅（《相應部》35.28）。「涅槃」這個詞，意思正是如此。還有，希臘的辯論有兩邊，佛教傳統則算出三邊。針對巴門尼德，它否認有任何東西是恆常的。針對克拉底魯那種極端，它肯定條件會可靠地產生它們的結果。它自己的立場是中間那一個：有連續，而沒有同一（佛法與西方哲學 D5）。

further.n_zh: 河的說法成為諺語的地方，以及柏拉圖反對徹底流變的論證。

further.n_zh: 川上的孔子，附兩家公版英譯。

lessons.title: Do We Have Free Will?
lessons.blurb_en: If every event follows from earlier events by fixed laws, your choices were settled before you were born. Three ways of living with that thought, and a fourth that says it does not matter.
lessons.blurb_zh: 如果每個事件都依固定的定律從先前的事件而來，你的選擇在你出生之前就已經定了。有三種方式與這個想法共處，還有第四種說：這根本無關緊要。
lessons.big_en: The dispute about free will is largely a dispute about what freedom is. If it means being uncaused, we probably lack it. If it means acting from our own reasons without constraint, we often have it, whatever physics says.
lessons.big_zh: 關於自由意志的爭論，大體上是在爭「自由是什麼」。如果它的意思是「不被任何原因造成」，我們大概沒有。如果它的意思是「不受強制、出於自己的理由而行動」，那麼不管物理學怎麼說，我們常常是有的。

paras.en: This morning you chose what to eat. It felt as though the choice was yours, and as though you could have taken the other thing. Almost everything we care about in human life rests on that feeling. We praise people and blame them, make promises and hold grudges, deliberate and regret, all on the assumption that what a person does is up to that person. The difficulty is that we also believe every event has a cause. Your choice was an event in your brain. It had causes, which had causes of their own, and the chain runs back to a time before you existed. If so, in what sense was the choice up to you?
paras.zh: 今天早上，你選了要吃什麼。感覺上，這個選擇是你的，而且你本來可以拿另一樣。人類生活裡我們在乎的幾乎一切，都建立在這個感覺上。我們稱讚人、責備人，許下承諾、懷著怨恨，斟酌與後悔，全都預設了：一個人做什麼，取決於這個人自己。困難在於，我們同時也相信每個事件都有原因。你的選擇是你腦中的一個事件。它有原因，那些原因又有自己的原因；這條鏈子一路回溯到你存在之前。如果是這樣，這個選擇在什麼意義上「取決於你」？

paras.en: The clearest statement of the worry was written in 1814 by the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace. “We ought then to regard the present state of the universe as the effect of its anterior state and as the cause of the one which is to follow.” Imagine an intelligence that knew, at one instant, all the forces of nature and the position of every particle, and that was vast enough to calculate with them. “For it, nothing would be uncertain and the future, as the past, would be present to its eyes.” This is determinism: given the state of the world at one time and the laws of nature, only one future is possible. Laplace’s intelligence, which later writers called his demon, would know what you will have for breakfast on a morning ten years from now.
paras.zh: 把這個憂慮說得最清楚的，是法國數學家拉普拉斯在 1814 年寫下的一段話。「因此，我們應當把宇宙的現在狀態，看作它先前狀態的結果，以及隨後狀態的原因。」設想有一個智能，在某一瞬間知道自然界所有的力，以及每一個粒子的位置，並且龐大到足以拿這些資料來計算。「對它來說，沒有什麼是不確定的；未來就像過去一樣，會呈現在它眼前。」這就是決定論：給定世界在某一時刻的狀態，加上自然定律，就只有一個未來是可能的。拉普拉斯的這個智能，後人稱之為他的「惡魔」，會知道十年後的某個早上你要吃什麼早餐。

essay.h_en: Spinoza: the stone that thinks it flies
essay.h_zh: 史賓諾莎：以為自己在飛的石頭

paras.en: A century and a half earlier, Baruch Spinoza had drawn the conclusion without flinching. “Nothing in the universe is contingent,” he wrote. Everything that happens follows from the nature of things with the same necessity by which the angles of a triangle add up to two right angles. People believe otherwise for a reason he states exactly: “men are mistaken in thinking themselves free; their opinion is made up of consciousness of their own actions, and ignorance of the causes by which they are conditioned.” We notice our desires and do not notice where they come from. “Thus an infant believes that of its own free will it desires milk, an angry child believes that it freely desires vengeance, a timid child believes that it freely desires to run away.” In a letter he imagined a stone that became conscious while flying through the air. It would suppose, he said, that it was moving because it wished to.
paras.zh: 比這早一個半世紀，史賓諾莎就毫不退縮地得出了這個結論。他寫道：「宇宙中沒有任何東西是偶然的。」發生的一切，都從事物的本性必然地推出，就像三角形的內角和等於兩個直角那樣必然。人們之所以不這麼相信，他把理由說得很精確：「人們自以為自由，這是錯的；他們這個意見的由來，是意識到自己的行動，卻不知道決定這些行動的原因。」我們察覺到自己的欲望，卻沒有察覺它們從哪裡來。「於是嬰兒相信，他是憑自己的自由意志想喝奶；生氣的孩子相信，他是自由地想要報復；膽小的孩子相信，他是自由地想要逃跑。」在一封信裡，他設想有一顆石頭在空中飛的時候有了意識。他說，那顆石頭會以為，自己是因為想動才動的。

paras.en: Suppose determinism is true. Then, the argument runs, nobody could ever have done anything other than what he did. The thief could not have refrained and the hero could not have run away. It seems unfair to blame a person for what he could not help, and pointless to praise him. Philosophers who accept this reasoning are called hard determinists. They conclude that moral responsibility, in the sense of deserving reward or punishment, is an illusion, and that we should treat wrongdoers as we treat the sick or the dangerous, with treatment and restraint and without resentment. Spinoza recommended exactly that attitude: not to laugh at human actions, or weep at them, or hate them, but to understand them.
paras.zh: 假設決定論是真的。那麼，這個論證說，從來沒有人能做出他實際所做之外的任何事。小偷不可能忍住不偷，英雄不可能逃跑。為了一個人不由自主的事而責備他，似乎不公平；稱讚他，似乎也沒有意義。接受這個推理的哲學家，稱為硬決定論者。他們的結論是：道德責任，就「理應受賞或受罰」這個意思而言，是一個幻覺；我們對待做錯事的人，應該像對待病人或危險的人那樣，給予治療與約束，而不帶怨恨。史賓諾莎建議的正是這種態度：對人的行為，不嘲笑，不哀嘆，不憎恨，而是去理解。

paras.en: One reply accepts that determinism and freedom cannot both be true, and concludes that determinism is false. Those who take this line are called libertarians, in a sense that has nothing to do with politics. They hold that when I choose, I start a new chain of causes that was not fixed by anything earlier. The ancient atomist Epicurus thought that atoms occasionally swerve for no reason, and some modern writers appeal to the indeterminacy of quantum physics. The standing objection is that chance is no better than necessity. If my arm moves because of a random event in a neuron, the movement is a twitch, and a twitch is not a choice.
paras.zh: 一種回應承認決定論與自由不可能同時為真，然後推斷：決定論是假的。採取這條路線的人稱為自由意志論者（libertarian，這個詞在這裡跟政治無關）。他們主張，當我做選擇的時候，我開啟了一條新的因果鏈，它不是由先前的任何東西決定的。古代的原子論者伊比鳩魯認為，原子偶爾會毫無理由地偏斜；有些現代作者則訴諸量子物理的不確定性。對這條路線的一貫反駁是：機遇並不比必然好。如果我的手臂是因為神經元裡的一個隨機事件而動，那個動作只是抽搐，而抽搐不是選擇。

paras.en: The other reply is that the conflict was never real. This is compatibilism, and its classic statement is Hume’s: “By liberty, then, we can only mean a power of acting or not acting, according to the determinations of the will; that is, if we choose to remain at rest, we may; if we choose to move, we also may.” Freedom, on this view, is the absence of constraint. A prisoner in chains is unfree. So is a person at gunpoint, or in the grip of a compulsion he would give anything to be rid of. A person who does what he wants, for his own reasons, is free, and it makes no difference that his wants have causes. Indeed they had better have causes, since an action that sprang from nothing in my character would hardly be mine. The contemporary philosopher Harry Frankfurt refined the idea. What matters is whether the desire I act on is one that I want to have, as the addict’s craving is not.
paras.zh: 另一種回應是：衝突從來就不是真的。這是相容論，它的經典陳述出自休謨：「那麼，所謂自由，我們只能是指一種依照意志的決定而行動或不行動的能力；也就是說，如果我們選擇保持靜止，我們可以；如果我們選擇移動，我們也可以。」照這個看法，自由就是沒有強制。戴著鎖鍊的囚犯是不自由的。被槍指著的人也是，被某種他願意付出一切代價擺脫的強迫性衝動攫住的人也是。一個人做他想做的事、出於他自己的理由，就是自由的；至於他的欲望有原因，這毫無差別。事實上，它們最好有原因：一個不是從我的性格中任何東西產生的行動，很難說是我的行動。當代哲學家法蘭克福把這個想法磨得更細：要緊的是，我據以行動的那個欲望，是不是一個我「想要擁有」的欲望；而成癮者的渴求並不是。

essay.h_en: What is decreed and what is up to me

paras.en: Chinese philosophers argued about ming (命), which means both “fate” and “what is decreed.” The Mohists attacked fatalism as a doctrine that ruins people. If the rich are fated to be rich and the poor to be poor, then, as the fatalists say, effort is useless, and a ruler who believes it will stop governing and a farmer will stop plowing. Mozi called this teaching a great harm to the world. Mencius drew a finer line. Some things, he said, are such that “if you seek them you get them, and if you neglect them you lose them,” because the seeking is within yourself. Others depend on what is outside, and there, seeking is no help to getting. Virtue is of the first kind and wealth and long life are of the second. This is not a theory of causation. It is closer to the compatibilist’s point, that the question of what is in my power can be answered by looking at what responds to my effort, without first settling the metaphysics.
paras.zh: 中國哲學家爭論的是「命」，這個字既指「命運」，也指「被決定的」。墨家攻擊宿命論，說它是一種毀人的學說。如果富人命中注定富、窮人命中注定窮，那麼正如主張有命的人所說，努力是沒有用的；相信這一套的君主會不再治理，農夫會不再耕田。墨子稱這種說法是「天下之大害」。孟子畫了一條更細的線。他說，有些東西是「求則得之，舍則失之」的，因為「求在我者也」。另一些取決於外在，在那裡，「求無益於得也」。德行屬於第一類，富貴與長壽屬於第二類。這不是一套因果理論。它比較接近相容論者的論點：要回答「什麼在我的能力之內」，可以看什麼東西會回應我的努力，而不必先把形上學解決。

paras.en: In 1983 the physiologist Benjamin Libet asked volunteers to flex a wrist whenever they felt like it and to note the moment at which they became aware of the urge. Electrodes on the scalp showed a build-up of activity in the brain about half a second before the movement, and about a third of a second before the reported decision. Many people took this as proof that the conscious will arrives too late to cause anything. The interpretation is disputed. The actions were trivial and unreasoned, the timing of an inner event is hard to report, and later work suggests that the early signal may reflect background fluctuation and not a decision already made. A compatibilist adds that the result would not matter in any case. A decision made by my brain is a decision made by me.
paras.zh: 1983 年，生理學家利貝特請受試者想動的時候就彎一下手腕，並且記下自己察覺到那股衝動的時刻。頭皮上的電極顯示，在動作之前大約半秒，腦中就出現了活動的累積；這比受試者回報的「決定」時刻，早了大約三分之一秒。許多人把這當作證據，證明有意識的意志來得太晚，不可能是任何事的原因。這種解讀有爭議。那些動作是瑣碎而不涉及理由的；內在事件的時間點很難回報；後來的研究也顯示，早期的訊號反映的可能是背景波動，而不是一個已經做出的決定。相容論者還會補一句：無論如何，這個結果都無關緊要。由我的大腦做出的決定，就是由我做出的決定。

paras.en: Suppose you became convinced that there is no free will. What would you do differently? You would still have to decide what to eat. You could not sit back and wait to see what you were determined to do, since sitting back would be one of the options. P. F. Strawson argued in 1962 that our practices of gratitude, resentment, and forgiveness do not rest on a theory that might be refuted. They are part of what it is to live with other people, and no argument could lead us to give them up wholesale. What can change is their tone. A person who sees how much of anyone’s character was shaped by things he did not choose may judge others more gently and take less credit for himself. On that modest conclusion Spinoza, Hume, Mencius, and the Buddha are closer together than their theories would lead one to expect.
paras.zh: 假設你被說服了，相信沒有自由意志。你會有什麼不同的做法？你還是得決定吃什麼。你沒辦法往後一靠，等著看自己「被決定」去做什麼，因為往後一靠也是選項之一。史陶生在 1962 年論證：我們感激、怨恨與寬恕的種種做法，並不是建立在一個可能被駁倒的理論上。它們是「跟別人一起生活」這件事的一部分，沒有哪個論證能讓我們把它們全盤放棄。能改變的是它們的調子。一個人如果看清，任何人的性格有多少是由他沒有選擇的東西塑造的，他對別人的判斷也許會溫和一些，對自己的功勞也會少居一些。在這個平實的結論上，史賓諾莎、休謨、孟子與佛陀彼此的距離，比他們的理論讓人預期的要近。

lab.title_en: Try it: Laplace’s table
lab.title_zh: 親手做一次：拉普拉斯的球桌
lab.lead_en: A small universe of six balls that obeys fixed laws. Run it, rewind it, and run it again. Then change one ball by a hundredth of a degree. After that, the demon tries to predict you.
lab.lead_zh: 一個由六顆球組成的小宇宙，遵守固定的定律。讓它跑一次，倒回去，再跑一次。然後把其中一顆球的方向改動百分之一度。之後，換惡魔來預測你。

start.en: Press “Run the universe.” Watch where the red ball ends up.
start.zh: 按「讓宇宙運行」。看紅球最後停在哪裡。

ran.en: The red ball finished on the {side} side. Rewind and run it again.
ran.zh: 紅球最後停在{side_zh}邊。倒回去，再跑一次。

same.en: Exactly the same, to the last decimal place, however many times you replay it. Given the starting state and the laws, there was only one possible outcome. This is what determinism means.
same.zh: 一模一樣，連最後一位小數都相同，不管你重播幾次。給定初始狀態與定律，可能的結果只有一個。這就是決定論的意思。

nudged.en: You turned the red ball’s first direction by one hundredth of a degree, and it now finishes somewhere else. The world is still perfectly determined. It has become impossible to predict without perfect knowledge. Laplace’s demon needs every position to infinitely many decimal places.
nudged.zh: 你把紅球最初的方向轉了百分之一度，它現在停在別的地方了。這個世界仍然是完全被決定的。只是沒有完美的知識，就變得無法預測。拉普拉斯的惡魔，需要每一個位置精確到無窮多位小數。

q.en: Now you. The demon has studied you and sealed its prediction in an envelope. Choose a hand.
q.zh: 現在輪到你。惡魔研究過你，把它的預測封在信封裡了。選一隻手。

open.en: The envelope says: “{pick}.” The demon was right.
open.zh: 信封裡寫著：「{pick_zh}。」惡魔猜對了。

confess.en: This demon cheated. It wrote the word after you chose, and it would have been right whichever hand you picked. A real demon would have to write first, and for that it would need the state of every particle in your brain, more exactly than any instrument could ever measure. The philosophical question is whether its failure is only practical. If the information existed, would your choice already be in the envelope?
confess.zh: 這個惡魔作弊了。它是在你選完之後才寫字的；不管你選哪一隻手，它都會「猜對」。真正的惡魔必須先寫，而要做到這一點，它需要你腦中每一個粒子的狀態，精確到任何儀器都量不到的程度。哲學上的問題是：它的失敗是不是僅僅出於實際上的困難？如果那份資訊存在，你的選擇是不是早就在信封裡了？

q.en: Where do you stand?
q.zh: 你站在哪一邊？

t.en: Everything is determined, so free will is an illusion.
t.zh: 一切都被決定了，所以自由意志是幻覺。

r.en: You are with Spinoza. The cost is desert: no one ever truly deserves praise or blame, including the people you love and the people who have wronged you. Ask whether you can actually take up that attitude toward someone who has betrayed you, and whether you would want to.
r.zh: 你跟史賓諾莎站在一起。代價是「應得」：沒有人真正應得稱讚或責備，包括你愛的人，也包括對不起你的人。問問自己：面對一個背叛過你的人，你真的採取得了這種態度嗎？你會想要這樣嗎？

t.en: I am free, so not everything is determined.
t.zh: 我是自由的，所以並非一切都被決定。

r.en: You hold that your choices are not fixed by the past. Then something in you must act without being caused to, and you owe an account of what that is. If it is chance, the choice is not yours. If it is your character and reasons, those have a history. The demand is for a cause that is yours and has no causes itself.
r.zh: 你主張你的選擇不是由過去決定的。那麼你裡面就必須有某個東西，不被任何原因造成而行動；而你欠一個說明：那是什麼？如果是機遇，這個選擇就不是你的。如果是你的性格與理由，它們是有來歷的。這裡要求的是一個「屬於你、而本身沒有原因」的原因。

t.en: Both. Freedom is acting from my own reasons, and that is compatible with determinism.
t.zh: 兩者皆是。自由就是出於我自己的理由而行動，這跟決定論是相容的。

r.en: This is the majority view among philosophers today. The difficulty is the manipulation case. Suppose a neuroscientist had secretly installed all your desires and reasons. You would still act from them without constraint, and few would call you free. You must say how being shaped by genes and upbringing differs from that.
r.zh: 這是今天哲學家當中的多數看法。困難在於「操控」的案例。假設有一位神經科學家偷偷植入了你全部的欲望與理由。你仍然是出於它們、不受強制地行動；可是很少有人會說你是自由的。你必須說明：被基因與教養塑造，跟這個案例差在哪裡？

t.en: Neither determinism nor chance leaves room for the freedom we want.
t.zh: 不管是決定論還是機遇，都沒有留下空間給我們想要的那種自由。

r.en: This is the position of Galen Strawson. To be truly responsible for what you do, you would have to be responsible for the way you are, and for that you would have had to make yourself, which nothing can do. The view is hard to refute. Its defenders tend to live exactly like everyone else, and they regard that as a fact about human psychology that leaves the argument untouched.
r.zh: 這是蓋倫・史陶生的立場。要為你所做的事真正負責，你就得為「你是什麼樣的人」負責；而要做到這一點，你得先造出你自己，這是任何東西都辦不到的。這個看法很難駁倒。為它辯護的人，日子過得往往跟其他人一模一樣；而他們認為，那只是關於人類心理的一個事實，論證本身並沒有因此受到影響。

argument.lead_en: The strongest argument that determinism rules out freedom was given its modern form by Peter van Inwagen in 1983. It is called the consequence argument. Click a step to see what can be said against it.
argument.lead_zh: 主張「決定論排除自由」的最強論證，由范因瓦根在 1983 年給了它現代的形式，稱為「後果論證」。點任何一步，看看別人可以怎麼反對它。

steps.en: No one has any control over what happened before he was born, or over what the laws of nature are.
steps.zh: 沒有人能控制自己出生之前發生的事，也沒有人能控制自然定律是什麼。
steps.ob_en: Hardly deniable.
steps.ob_zh: 幾乎無法否認。

steps.en: If determinism is true, everything we do is a necessary consequence of the distant past together with the laws of nature.
steps.zh: 如果決定論為真，我們所做的一切，都是遙遠的過去加上自然定律的必然後果。
steps.ob_en: This is what determinism says. Whether determinism is true is a question for physics, and the present evidence is mixed.
steps.ob_zh: 這就是決定論的內容。決定論是不是真的，是物理學的問題；目前的證據是分歧的。

steps.en: If we have no control over certain things, we have no control over their necessary consequences.
steps.zh: 如果我們對某些事沒有控制力，我們對它們的必然後果也沒有控制力。
steps.ob_en: This is the step most often attacked. The compatibilist replies that it mistakes what control is. I control an outcome when it depends on my deliberation, so that had I judged differently, it would have been different. That dependence exists in a determined world. The past produced my act by way of my reasons, and passing through me is what makes it mine.
steps.ob_zh: 這是最常被攻擊的一步。相容論者回答說，它把「控制」弄錯了。當一個結果取決於我的斟酌——假如我的判斷不同，結果就會不同——我就控制了它。這種依賴關係，在一個被決定的世界裡照樣存在。過去是「經由」我的理由產生了我的行動；而它經過我，正是使它成為「我的」的原因。

steps.en: Therefore, if determinism is true, we have no control over what we do.
steps.zh: 所以，如果決定論為真，我們對自己所做的事沒有控制力。
steps.ob_en: Accepted by hard determinists and by libertarians, who then disagree about whether determinism is true. Rejected by compatibilists, who think the argument shows only that we did not create ourselves from nothing, which nobody supposed.
steps.ob_zh: 硬決定論者與自由意志論者都接受這個結論，然後對決定論是否為真意見相左。相容論者拒絕它；他們認為這個論證只證明了我們不是從無中創造出自己的，而本來就沒有人這麼以為。

source.work: Laplace, A Philosophical Essay on Probabilities (1814); Spinoza, Ethics (1677)
source.work_zh: 拉普拉斯《機率的哲學論文》；史賓諾莎《倫理學》
source.tr: Laplace translated by F. W. Truscott and F. L. Emory; Spinoza translated by R. H. M. Elwes (both public domain)
source.lead_en: The first passage states determinism as a physicist sees it. The second explains why, if it is true, we do not feel it.
source.lead_zh: 第一段陳述的是物理學家眼中的決定論。第二段解釋：如果它是真的，我們為什麼感覺不到。

passages.en: Given for one instant an intelligence which could comprehend all the forces by which nature is animated and the respective situation of the beings who compose it—an intelligence sufficiently vast to submit these data to analysis—it would embrace in the same formula the movements of the greatest bodies of the universe and those of the lightest atom; for it, nothing would be uncertain and the future, as the past, would be present to its eyes.
passages.zh: 假定有一個智能，在某一瞬間能夠掌握使自然運轉的一切的力，以及構成自然的種種存在物各自的位置；這個智能又龐大到足以把這些資料付諸分析；那麼它就能用同一個公式，囊括宇宙中最大的物體與最輕的原子的運動。對它來說，沒有什麼是不確定的；未來就像過去一樣，會呈現在它眼前。
passages.note_en: Two things are worth noticing. The passage comes from a book about probability, and Laplace’s purpose is to explain why we need probabilities at all: because we are not that intelligence. The demon is a way of saying that chance is a measure of our ignorance. And the sentence is conditional. He does not claim that such a mind exists. He claims that the future is fixed whether or not anyone can read it. (“Analysis” here means mathematical calculation.)
passages.note_zh: 有兩件事值得注意。這段話出自一本談機率的書，拉普拉斯的目的是解釋我們到底為什麼需要機率：因為我們不是那個智能。惡魔是一種說法，意思是機遇是我們無知程度的度量。而且這個句子是條件句。他並沒有宣稱這樣的心靈存在。他主張的是：不管有沒有人讀得出來，未來都是固定的。（這裡的 analysis 是「數學計算」的意思。）

passages.ref: Spinoza, Ethics, Part III, proposition 2, scholium
passages.en: Thus an infant believes that of its own free will it desires milk, an angry child believes that it freely desires vengeance, a timid child believes that it freely desires to run away; further, a drunken man believes that he utters from the free decision of his mind words which, when he is sober, he would willingly have withheld.
passages.zh: 於是嬰兒相信，他是憑自己的自由意志想喝奶；生氣的孩子相信，他是自由地想要報復；膽小的孩子相信，他是自由地想要逃跑；還有，喝醉的人相信，他是出於心靈的自由決定而說出那些話，而那些話，他清醒的時候是寧願沒說出口的。
passages.note_en: The examples are chosen with care. In each we, the onlookers, can see the cause plainly, and the person cannot. Spinoza’s suggestion is that the sober adult stands to his own choices as the drunkard stands to his words. The feeling of freedom is real, and it is evidence only that we are aware of wanting and unaware of why. A scholium is a note attached to a formal proof, and Spinoza often put his most vivid writing there.
passages.note_zh: 這些例子是仔細挑過的。在每一個例子裡，我們這些旁觀者把原因看得清清楚楚，當事人卻看不見。史賓諾莎的暗示是：清醒的成年人對於自己的選擇，就像醉漢對於自己說的話。「自由」的感覺是真實的；但它只能證明，我們察覺到自己想要，卻沒察覺到為什麼想要。scholium（附釋）是附在正式證明之後的註記，史賓諾莎常把他最生動的文字放在那裡。

items.o_en: I know that I am free, because I experience it every time I choose. No argument can be more certain than that experience.
items.o_zh: 我知道我是自由的，因為每次做選擇的時候我都經驗到它。沒有任何論證能比這個經驗更確定。
items.r_en: Samuel Johnson put it in one line: “Sir, we know our will is free, and there’s an end on’t.” Spinoza’s answer is the drunkard. What we experience is the wanting and the doing. We do not experience the absence of causes, since an absence is not the kind of thing that can be felt. The experience is the same whether determinism is true or false, and so it cannot decide between them.
items.r_zh: 山繆・約翰遜用一句話說完了：「先生，我們知道自己的意志是自由的，這事就到此為止。」史賓諾莎的回答是那個醉漢。我們經驗到的是「想要」與「去做」。我們並沒有經驗到「沒有原因」，因為「沒有」不是一種可以被感覺到的東西。不管決定論是真是假，這個經驗都一樣；所以它無法在兩者之間做出裁決。

items.o_en: Quantum physics has shown that the world is not deterministic. The problem has been dissolved by science.
items.o_zh: 量子物理已經證明世界不是決定論的。這個問題已經被科學化解了。
items.r_en: Whether quantum theory is indeterministic depends on how it is interpreted, and physicists disagree. Suppose it is. The uncertainty of a single atom is mostly swamped at the scale of neurons, and where it is not, it gives us randomness. A decision that came from the unpredictable decay of a particle would be no more mine than one that came from the laws of Newton. Indeterminism removes one threat and does nothing to supply control.
items.r_zh: 量子理論是不是非決定論的，取決於怎麼詮釋它，而物理學家對此意見不一。就假設它是吧。單一原子的不確定性，到了神經元的尺度多半已經被淹沒；沒被淹沒的地方，它給我們的是隨機。一個出自粒子不可預測的衰變的決定，並不比一個出自牛頓定律的決定更屬於我。非決定論移除了一個威脅，卻絲毫沒有提供控制力。

items.o_en: If people come to believe there is no free will, they will behave worse. So the doctrine is dangerous, whatever its truth.
items.o_zh: 如果人們開始相信沒有自由意志，他們的行為會變糟。所以不管這個學說是真是假，它都是危險的。
items.r_en: The Mohists said this of fatalism, and some experiments have suggested that people cheat more after reading arguments against free will, though the findings have not held up well. Two replies are available. Determinism is not fatalism: it says that your efforts are among the causes of what happens, so effort makes all the difference. And the consequences of believing a thing are not evidence for or against it. If the truth is uncomfortable, the remedy is to understand it properly.
items.r_zh: 墨家對宿命論說過這樣的話；也有一些實驗顯示，人讀了反對自由意志的論證之後比較會作弊，雖然這些發現後來不太站得住。有兩個回應。決定論不是宿命論：它說你的努力是事情發生的原因之一，所以努力造成一切差別。還有，相信一件事會有什麼後果，並不是支持或反對這件事的證據。如果真相令人不舒服，解方是把它理解對。

said.claim: “A man can do what he wants, but not want what he wants.” (Einstein)
said.claim_zh: 「人能做他想做的，卻不能想要他所想要的。」（愛因斯坦）
said.en: Einstein did say this, and said whose it was. In a statement of his beliefs written around 1932 he quoted it as Schopenhauer’s saying and added that it had consoled him since his youth and taught him patience with other people. The thought comes from Schopenhauer’s prize essay On the Freedom of the Will (1839). It is a fair summary of the compatibilist’s premise and the hard determinist’s conclusion at once.
said.zh: 愛因斯坦確實說過這句話，而且說明了它是誰的。在大約 1932 年寫下的一篇信念自述裡，他把它當作叔本華的話來引用，並且補充說，這句話從他年輕時就安慰著他，教他對別人有耐心。這個想法出自叔本華的得獎論文《論意志的自由》（1839）。它同時相當貼切地概括了相容論者的前提，以及硬決定論者的結論。

terms.d_en: The thesis that the state of the world at one time, with the laws of nature, fixes its state at every later time.
terms.d_zh: 主張世界在某一時刻的狀態加上自然定律，就決定了它在此後每一時刻的狀態。

terms.d_en: The view that what will happen will happen whatever we do. Distinct from determinism, on which what we do is among the causes.
terms.d_zh: 主張不管我們做什麼，該發生的都會發生。與決定論不同：依決定論，我們所做的事正是原因之一。

terms.d_en: The view that free will and determinism can both be true.
terms.d_zh: 主張自由意志與決定論可以同時為真。

terms.d_en: The view that they cannot. It includes hard determinism and libertarianism.
terms.d_zh: 主張兩者不能同時為真。包括硬決定論與自由意志論。

terms.d_en: In metaphysics, the view that we are free and that determinism is therefore false.
terms.d_zh: 在形上學裡，指主張我們是自由的、因此決定論為假的看法。

terms.d_en: The view that determinism is true and that free will is therefore an illusion.
terms.d_zh: 主張決定論為真、因此自由意志是幻覺的看法。

terms.d_en: The condition of deserving praise or blame for what one does.
terms.d_zh: 對自己所做的事理應受到稱讚或責備的狀態。

terms.d_en: Such that it could have been otherwise; the opposite of necessary.
terms.d_zh: 本來可以是別的樣子；「必然」的反面。

terms.d_en: P. F. Strawson’s term for resentment, gratitude, indignation, and the like, which we feel toward persons as responsible agents.
terms.d_zh: 史陶生的術語，指怨恨、感激、義憤之類，我們把人當作負責的行為者時對他們產生的感受。

vocab.eg: Almost everything we care about rests on that feeling.
vocab.eg_zh: 我們在乎的幾乎一切，都建立在那個感覺上。

vocab.eg: We assume that what a person does is up to that person.
vocab.eg_zh: 我們預設，一個人做什麼取決於這個人自己。

vocab.eg: Spinoza drew the conclusion without flinching.
vocab.eg_zh: 史賓諾莎毫不退縮地得出了這個結論。

vocab.eg: The thief could not have refrained.
vocab.eg_zh: 小偷不可能忍住不偷。

vocab.eg: It seems unfair to blame a person for what he could not help.
vocab.eg_zh: 為了一個人不由自主的事而責備他，似乎不公平。

vocab.eg: Those who take this line are called libertarians.
vocab.eg_zh: 採取這條路線的人，稱為自由意志論者。

vocab.eg: A person in the grip of a compulsion is not free.
vocab.eg_zh: 被強迫性衝動攫住的人，是不自由的。

vocab.eg: He would give anything to be rid of it.
vocab.eg_zh: 他願意付出一切代價擺脫它。

vocab.eg: No argument could lead us to give them up wholesale.
vocab.eg_zh: 沒有哪個論證能讓我們把它們全盤放棄。

vocab.eg: He may take less credit for himself.
vocab.eg_zh: 他對自己的功勞也會少居一些。

quiz.q: What does determinism claim?
options: The state of the world at one time, with the laws of nature, allows only one future.
Whatever happens is the will of the gods.
Nothing can be predicted.
People always act selfishly.

quiz.q: Why, according to Spinoza, do people believe they are free?
options: They are conscious of their actions and ignorant of the causes.
They have been taught to by priests.
They can predict their own choices.
They are in fact free.

quiz.q: What is freedom, on Hume’s compatibilist account?
options: The power to act or not act according to the determinations of one’s will.
The absence of all causes.
Acting at random.
Obedience to the law.

quiz.q: Why does quantum indeterminacy not obviously rescue free will?
options: A random event is no more under my control than a determined one.
Quantum physics has been refuted.
Atoms are not part of the brain.
It applies only to light.

quiz.q: What distinction does Mencius draw?
options: Between what is gained by seeking because it lies within oneself, and what depends on things outside.
Between gods and human beings.
Between rich people and poor people.
Between past lives and future lives.

write.en: Describe a decision you made that felt entirely free. Then list three things you did not choose that helped to produce it.
write.zh: 描述一個你做過、感覺上完全自由的決定。然後列出三樣不是你選擇的、卻促成了這個決定的東西。

write.en: Which of the four positions in the exercise is closest to yours? Defend it in about 150 words against the objection printed under it.
write.zh: 練習裡的四個立場，哪一個最接近你的？用大約 150 個英文字，針對它底下印的那個反駁為它辯護。

write.en: A student says: “I can’t help being lazy. It’s how I was made.” As a teacher, how would you answer, and which philosopher would you be agreeing with?
write.zh: 一個學生說：「我就是懶，沒辦法，我天生就這樣。」身為老師，你會怎麼回答？你這樣回答，是在同意哪一位哲學家？

paras.en: The Buddha lived among teachers who held nearly every position in this debate, and he rejected the extremes on practical grounds. One discourse lists three views that, when pressed, lead to inaction: that everything a person experiences is caused by past deeds, that everything is caused by the creative act of a supreme god, and that everything happens without cause or condition (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.61). If any of them were true, he says, there would be no reason to make an effort to do this and avoid that. The first of the three is notable, because it is a view about karma. The Buddha denies that the present is wholly fixed by past action.
paras.zh: 佛陀生活的時代，幾乎每一種立場都有老師在主張；而他基於實踐的理由，拒絕了那些極端。有一部經列出三種見解，說它們一經追問，就會歸結為無所作為：一個人所經驗的一切都由過去的行為造成；一切都由至高之神的創造造成；一切都無因無緣地發生（《增支部》3.61）。他說，如果其中任何一種是真的，人就沒有理由努力去做這個、避免那個。三者當中的第一種值得注意，因為那是一種關於業的見解。佛陀否認現在完全由過去的業所決定。

paras.en: What he affirms looks like compatibilism reached by another road. Actions arise from conditions, including intention, and intention is itself conditioned. Nothing stands outside the causal order, and there is no self behind the will to do the choosing. Yet when a brahmin tells him that there is no such thing as acting on one’s own initiative, the Buddha asks how a man who has just walked up to him of his own accord can say so. “Is there an element of initiative?” There is. And since there is, beings who initiate actions are found (Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.38). Karma on this account is a condition that can be worked with. The whole path assumes that understanding the causes of one’s states changes what those causes produce, and Spinoza built the last part of his Ethics on the same assumption. On the Buddhist view, freedom has to be gained by training. One comes to be less driven by craving and aversion as one sees more clearly how they arise (Dharma and the West, D17).
paras.zh: 他肯定的東西，看起來像是從另一條路走到的相容論。行為從條件生起，條件包括「思」（意圖），而意圖本身也是有條件的。沒有任何東西站在因果秩序之外，意志的背後也沒有一個「我」在做選擇。然而，當一位婆羅門告訴他「沒有所謂出於自己的主動而行動這回事」時，佛陀反問：一個剛剛自己走過來的人，怎麼能這樣說？「有沒有『發起』這個要素？」有。既然有，就找得到發起行動的眾生（《增支部》6.38）。照這個說法，業是一種可以拿來下工夫的條件。整條道路都預設：理解自己種種狀態的原因，會改變這些原因所產生的結果；而史賓諾莎《倫理學》的最後一部分，就建立在同一個預設上。依佛教的看法，自由必須靠修習才能獲得。人把貪與瞋怎麼生起看得愈清楚，受它們驅使的程度就愈低（佛法與西方哲學 D17）。

terms: the view that all is due to past action

further.t: Baruch Spinoza, Ethics, translated by R. H. M. Elwes: Part I, Appendix, and Part III, proposition 2
further.n_en: The Appendix is ten pages of plain prose and the best way into the book.
further.n_zh: 附錄是十頁平易的散文，也是進入這本書最好的入口。

further.t: David Hume, An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding, section VIII, “Of Liberty and Necessity”
further.n_en: The classic statement of compatibilism.
further.n_zh: 相容論的經典陳述。

further.t: P. F. Strawson, “Freedom and Resentment” (1962)
further.n_en: The essay that changed the subject from metaphysics to how we treat one another.
further.n_zh: 把這個題目從形上學轉到「我們怎麼對待彼此」的那篇文章。

further.t: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Free Will” and “Compatibilism”
Mozi, “Against Fatalism” (非命), and Mencius 7A3

lessons.title: What Is Time?
lessons.blurb_en: Augustine’s puzzle about the vanishing present, the quarrel over whether time flows, and what physics has done to the word “now.”
lessons.blurb_zh: 奧古斯丁關於「消失的現在」的難題、時間到底流不流動的爭論，以及物理學對「現在」這個詞做了什麼。
lessons.big_en: We live as though only the present exists and as though it moves. Each belief is very hard to defend. The alternative, that all times are equally real, fits the physics and leaves the experience of passage unexplained.
lessons.big_zh: 我們活得好像只有現在存在，而且好像現在會移動。這兩個信念都很難辯護。另一種看法是一切時刻同樣真實；它符合物理學，卻讓「流逝」的經驗沒有得到解釋。

paras.en: Around the year 400 Augustine of Hippo, writing the story of his life as a long prayer, stopped to ask a question that seemed to have nothing to do with it. “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not.” The remark is often quoted as a joke about philosophy. He meant it as a statement of the problem. We handle time without difficulty. We say that a speech was long, that a friend is late, that an hour has passed. Yet when we try to say what it is that passes, or where the long time is that we measured, the confidence disappears.
paras.zh: 大約在西元 400 年，希波的奧古斯丁正把自己一生的故事寫成一篇長長的禱告；他停下來，問了一個看似與此無關的問題。「那麼時間是什麼？沒有人問我，我是知道的；如果我想向發問的人解釋，我就不知道了。」這句話常被當成一個關於哲學的笑話來引用。他說這句話，是當作問題的陳述。我們處理時間毫無困難。我們說一場演講很長，說朋友遲到了，說一個小時過去了。可是，當我們試著說出「過去的那個東西」是什麼，或者我們量到的那段「很長的時間」在哪裡，那份把握就消失了。

paras.en: His argument is short. The past no longer exists, and the future does not yet exist. Only the present is. But how long is the present? This century is not all present, since most of its years are gone or still to come. The same is true of this year, this day, this hour. Take a single minute: part has already fled and part has not arrived. “If an instant of time be conceived, which cannot be divided into the smallest particles of moments, that alone is it, which may be called present. Which yet flies with such speed from future to past, as not to be lengthened out with the least stay.” He concludes: “The present hath no space.” So the past and future are nothing, and the present is a boundary with no extent. What, then, are we measuring when we say that a time was long?
paras.zh: 他的論證很短。過去已經不存在，未來還沒有存在。存在的只有現在。可是現在有多長？這個世紀並不是整個都是現在，因為它大部分的年頭不是已經過去，就是還沒到來。今年、今天、這個小時，也都一樣。拿單單一分鐘來說：一部分已經逃走，一部分還沒抵達。「如果設想有一個時間的瞬間，它不能再被分割成最小的片刻，那麼只有它才可以被稱為現在。然而它以如此的速度從未來飛向過去，以致於沒有絲毫的停留可以把它拉長。」他的結論是：「現在沒有長度。」所以過去與未來是無，而現在是一條沒有寬度的界線。那麼，當我們說一段時間很長的時候，我們量的是什麼？

paras.en: Augustine’s answer is that we measure something in ourselves. It is not strictly correct, he says, to speak of past, present, and future. One should speak of “a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future,” and these exist in the soul: “present of things past, memory; present of things present, sight; present of things future, expectation.” When I recite a psalm that I know by heart, my expectation reaches forward over the whole of it before I begin. As I go on, what was expected passes through my attention and becomes memory, until expectation is used up and all of it is memory. The long time I measure is a long memory or a long expectation. “It is in thee, my mind, that I measure times.” He called time a stretching of the mind.
paras.zh: 奧古斯丁的回答是：我們量的是自己裡面的東西。他說，嚴格來講，說「過去、現在、未來」並不恰當。應該說的是「過去事物的現在、現在事物的現在、未來事物的現在」，而這三者存在於靈魂之中：「過去事物的現在是記憶；現在事物的現在是直觀；未來事物的現在是期待。」當我背誦一首熟記的詩篇，在開口之前，我的期待就向前伸展，涵蓋了整首。隨著我往下背，被期待的東西通過我的注意力，變成記憶；直到期待用盡，全部成了記憶。我量到的那段「長時間」，是一段長的記憶，或一段長的期待。「我的心靈啊，我是在你裡面度量時間的。」他把時間稱為心靈的伸展。

essay.h_zh: 是一個東西，還是一種關係？

paras.en: Most philosophers have been unwilling to put time inside the mind, since the world surely had a history before there were minds. But they have disagreed about what sort of thing it is outside. Aristotle tied time to change. “Time is just this—number of motion in respect of ‘before’ and ‘after.’” Where nothing whatever changes, no time passes. Newton needed something firmer for his physics, and declared that “absolute, true, and mathematical time, of itself, and from its own nature flows equably without regard to anything external.” Time, for him, is like an empty container that would go on even if the universe were frozen. His rival Leibniz replied that this is a fiction. Time is the order in which events succeed one another, and to speak of time with no events in it is like speaking of a family tree with no people.
paras.zh: 多數哲學家不願意把時間放進心靈裡，因為在有心靈之前，世界肯定已經有了歷史。可是，時間在心靈之外是哪一種東西，他們意見不一。亞里斯多德把時間繫在變化上。「時間就是這個：就『先』與『後』而言的運動之數。」什麼都不變的地方，就沒有時間流逝。牛頓的物理學需要更堅實的東西；他宣稱：「絕對的、真實的、數學的時間，自身依其本性均勻地流逝，與任何外在的事物無關。」對他來說，時間像一個空的容器，就算宇宙凍結了，它也會繼續走。他的對手萊布尼茲回應說，這是虛構。時間是事件彼此相續的次序；談論「裡面沒有任何事件的時間」，就像談論「沒有任何人的族譜」。

paras.en: In 1908 the Cambridge philosopher J. M. E. McTaggart drew a distinction that has organized the debate ever since. Events can be ordered in two ways. In the first, each event is past, present, or future, and its position is always changing: the death of Socrates was once in the far future, became present, and has been sinking deeper into the past ever since. In the second, events are simply earlier or later than one another, and these relations never change. The death of Socrates is earlier than the birth of Augustine, and it always was and always will be.
paras.zh: 1908 年，劍橋的哲學家麥塔加畫出了一個區分，此後這場辯論一直照著它來組織。事件可以用兩種方式排序。在第一種裡，每個事件是過去的、現在的或未來的，而且它的位置一直在變：蘇格拉底之死曾經在遙遠的未來，後來成了現在，從那以後就愈來愈深地沉入過去。在第二種裡，事件之間只有「早於」或「晚於」的關係，而這些關係永遠不變。蘇格拉底之死早於奧古斯丁的出生；它過去一向如此，將來也永遠如此。

paras.en: The question is which ordering describes reality. On one view, often called presentism, only what is present exists, and the moving “now” is the most basic fact about the world. This agrees with experience and with Augustine’s premise. On the other view, called eternalism, all events are equally real, laid out along the dimension of time as places are laid out in space. “Now” is like “here,” a word that picks out wherever the speaker happens to be. Nothing moves. The first view has to explain what the present moves through and how fast, and the only available answer seems to be one second per second, which says nothing. The second has to explain why it feels so strongly as though time passes.
paras.zh: 問題是：哪一種排序描述的是實在？有一種看法，常稱為「現在論」，主張只有現在的東西存在，而那個移動的「現在」是關於世界最根本的事實。這符合經驗，也符合奧古斯丁的前提。另一種看法，稱為「永恆論」，主張所有事件同樣真實，沿著時間這個維度鋪開，就像各個地點在空間裡鋪開一樣。「現在」就像「這裡」，是一個指出說話者碰巧所在之處的詞。沒有任何東西在動。第一種看法必須解釋：「現在」穿過的是什麼？移動得多快？而唯一說得出來的答案似乎是「每秒一秒」，這等於什麼都沒說。第二種看法必須解釋：為什麼我們如此強烈地覺得時間在流逝？

essay.h_zh: 物理學對「現在」做了什麼

paras.en: Einstein’s theory of relativity, published in 1905, gave the eternalists their strongest argument. It showed that two observers moving relative to each other will disagree about which distant events are happening at the same moment, and that neither is wrong. There is no single “now” that spans the universe. If so, there can be no fact about which events, everywhere, are the present ones, and presentism appears to lose its subject. Late in life Einstein wrote to the family of a friend who had just died that for physicists “the distinction between past, present and future is only a stubbornly persistent illusion.”
paras.zh: 愛因斯坦在 1905 年發表的相對論，給了永恆論者最強的論證。它顯示：兩個彼此相對運動的觀察者，對於遠處的哪些事件「同時」發生，會有不同的判斷，而兩人都沒有錯。並沒有一個橫跨全宇宙的、單一的「現在」。若是如此，「全宇宙各處，哪些事件是現在的」這件事就沒有事實可言，而現在論似乎失去了它談論的對象。愛因斯坦晚年寫信給一位剛過世的朋友的家人，說對物理學家而言，「過去、現在與未來的區分，只是一個頑固持續的幻覺。」

paras.en: Physics also deepens a second puzzle. Its basic laws work equally well in either direction of time, and yet eggs break and do not unbreak, and we remember yesterday and not tomorrow. The standard explanation appeals to entropy: the universe began in an extremely orderly state and has been growing more disordered ever since, and the direction of increasing disorder is what we call the future. Why the universe began that way is not known.
paras.zh: 物理學還加深了第二個謎。它的基本定律在時間的兩個方向上同樣適用；然而蛋會破，不會復原，我們記得昨天，不記得明天。標準的解釋訴諸熵：宇宙從一個極度有序的狀態開始，此後一直變得更無序；而無序增加的方向，就是我們所說的未來。至於宇宙為什麼那樣開始，沒有人知道。

paras.en: Classical Chinese thought was little troubled by Augustine’s question and deeply interested in another. The word for the cosmos, 宇宙, is itself a theory of space and time. An early definition runs: “What has gone and what is to come, from of old until now, is called zhou (宙); the four directions with above and below are called yu (宇).” Time and space are named together as the two aspects of everything there is. Within that frame the pressing question was a practical one, what the moment calls for. The word 時 means “time,” “season,” and “timeliness,” and Mencius’s highest praise of Confucius was that he was “the sage who was timely” (聖之時者): he took office when it was right to take office and withdrew when it was right to withdraw. The Greek tradition treated time mainly as something to be measured or explained. Here it is something to be answered, as a farmer answers the seasons.
paras.zh: 中國古典思想很少為奧古斯丁的問題煩惱，卻對另一個問題深感興趣。「宇宙」這個詞本身，就是一套關於空間與時間的理論。有一個早期的定義是這樣的：「往古來今謂之宙，四方上下謂之宇。」時間與空間被並列命名，當作一切存在之物的兩個面向。在這個框架之內，迫切的問題是實踐上的：這個時刻要求什麼？「時」這個字的意思是「時間」「時節」，也是「合乎時宜」；孟子對孔子最高的讚語，就是「聖之時者也」：該出仕的時候出仕，該退的時候退。希臘傳統主要把時間當作要被度量或被解釋的東西。在這裡，它是要被回應的東西，就像農夫回應四季。

paras.en: The metaphysics of time seems remote from life, and it bears on how we live more directly than most of philosophy does. If only the present exists, then the dead are simply nothing, and so is everything you have done. If all times exist, then every moment of your life is permanently part of what there is, and its being over means only that it lies in an earlier part of the whole. People have found comfort in the second picture and some have been horrified by it. Augustine found his own answer by looking inward. He concluded that we are stretched across time, pulled between what we remember and what we expect, and that this stretching is what a human life is. With that conclusion the third unit ends. We have asked what a thing is, whether change is real, whether we are free, and what time is. In each case the plain facts, that ships are repaired, rivers flow, people choose, and the clock moves, turned out to be much less clear than they seemed.
paras.zh: 時間的形上學似乎離生活很遠；其實它對我們怎麼活的影響，比哲學的大部分內容都更直接。如果只有現在存在，那麼死者就是單純的無，你做過的一切也是。如果所有的時刻都存在，那麼你生命中的每一刻都永久地是「存在之物」的一部分；它「過去了」，只表示它位於整體當中較早的那一段。有人在第二幅圖像裡找到安慰，也有人被它嚇壞了。奧古斯丁靠著往內看，找到了他自己的答案。他的結論是：我們被拉開、橫跨在時間之上，在記得的與期待的之間被拉扯；而這個「被拉開」，就是人的一生。第三單元就以這個結論結束。我們問過：一樣東西是什麼？變化是不是真的？我們自由嗎？時間是什麼？在每一個問題上，那些明擺著的事實——船會被修補、河在流、人做選擇、時鐘在走——結果都遠不如看起來那麼清楚。

lab.title_en: Try it: how long is now?
lab.title_zh: 親手做一次：「現在」有多長？
lab.lead_en: Augustine’s argument, as something you can do. Start with the present year and keep looking closer. At every level the present turns out to contain a past and a future. Then measure a length of time, and ask yourself what it was that you measured.
lab.lead_zh: 把奧古斯丁的論證變成你可以動手做的事。從「今年」開始，一直往近處看。在每一層，「現在」結果都包含了一段過去與一段未來。然後量一段時間，再問問自己：你量的到底是什麼？

say.en: Is this whole year present? Some of its months are gone, and some have not come.
say.zh: 這一整年都是現在嗎？它有些月份已經過去，有些還沒來。

say.en: Then the present is this month. But its days, too, are either behind us or ahead.
say.zh: 那麼現在就是這個月。可是它的日子，同樣不是在我們後面，就是在前面。

say.en: Not even one day is present as a whole. Of its twenty-four hours, only one is now.
say.zh: 就連一天，也不是整個都是現在。它的二十四個小時裡，只有一個是此刻。

say.en: And that one hour passes in fleeting minutes. Whatever has flown is past, and whatever remains is to come.
say.zh: 而那一個小時，是在轉瞬即逝的分鐘裡過去的。已經飛走的是過去，還剩下的是未來。

say.en: Sixty seconds, of which fifty-nine are not now.
say.zh: 六十秒，其中五十九秒不是此刻。

say.en: A second is long enough for a hummingbird to beat its wings some fifty times. It has an earlier and a later part.
say.zh: 一秒鐘夠蜂鳥拍動翅膀五十次左右。它有較早的部分，也有較晚的部分。

say.en: Light travels three hundred kilometers in this. It can still be divided.
say.zh: 光在這段時間裡走了三百公里。它還可以再分。

end.en: You can go on as long as you like. Whatever has duration has parts, and of those parts only one can be present. “The present hath no space.” So where is the long time that you measure?
end.zh: 你愛繼續多久都可以。凡是有延續的東西，就有部分；而那些部分當中，只有一個可以是現在。「現在沒有長度。」那麼，你量到的那段長時間在哪裡？

q.en: Now measure a time. Press start, watch the light, and when it goes out, say how long it was on.
q.zh: 現在來量一段時間。按開始，看著那盞燈；等它熄了，說出它亮了多久。

after.en: The light was on for {actual} seconds, and you said {guess}. Notice what you did. When you made your estimate, the interval no longer existed. You measured your memory of it. That is Augustine’s point: “It is in thee, my mind, that I measure times.”
after.zh: 那盞燈亮了 {actual} 秒，你說的是 {guess} 秒。留意你剛才做了什麼。你估計的時候，那段時間已經不存在了。你量的是你對它的記憶。這就是奧古斯丁的重點：「我的心靈啊，我是在你裡面度量時間的。」

q.en: Two ways of ordering the same events. Switch between them and watch which facts change while you read.
q.zh: 同一串事件的兩種排法。在兩者之間切換，看看在你閱讀的時候，哪些事實在變。

t.en: Socrates drinks the hemlock
t.zh: 蘇格拉底喝下毒芹汁

t.en: Augustine writes the Confessions
t.zh: 奧古斯丁寫《懺悔錄》

t.en: Newton publishes the Principia
t.zh: 牛頓出版《原理》

t.en: You opened this page
t.zh: 你打開這個頁面

t.en: You finish this lesson
t.zh: 你讀完這一課

a.en: In this ordering every event has a position that is changing as you watch. The numbers below are getting larger. Many philosophers hold that this change is time itself.
a.zh: 在這種排序裡，每個事件的位置，就在你看著的時候正在改變。下面的數字愈來愈大。許多哲學家主張，這個改變就是時間本身。

b.en: In this ordering nothing changes, now or ever. These relations were true before any of the events happened and will be true when the sun has burned out. Other philosophers hold that this is all there is to time.
b.zh: 在這種排序裡，沒有任何東西改變，現在不變，永遠不變。這些關係在任何一個事件發生之前就是真的，等到太陽燃盡的時候也還是真的。另一些哲學家主張，時間就只是這樣而已。

q.en: Which picture of time do you accept?
q.zh: 你接受哪一幅時間的圖像？

t.en: Only the present exists.
t.zh: 只有現在存在。

r.en: This is the common-sense view and Augustine’s starting point. You then face his question, how long the present is, and Einstein’s, whose present it is. You must also say what makes it true that Socrates drank hemlock, if neither Socrates nor the hemlock exists in any sense.
r.zh: 這是常識的看法，也是奧古斯丁的出發點。於是你要面對他的問題：現在有多長？還有愛因斯坦的問題：那是誰的現在？你還必須說明：如果蘇格拉底與那杯毒芹汁在任何意義上都不存在，是什麼使「蘇格拉底喝了毒芹汁」為真？

t.en: The past and present exist, and the future does not yet.
t.zh: 過去與現在存在，未來還沒有。

opts.tag: The growing block · 成長塊體論

r.en: Reality grows as new moments are added, which keeps the past fixed and the future open. The awkward question is how you know that you are at the growing edge. People in the past, who on this view are real, believe that their moment is the latest one, and they are wrong.
r.zh: 隨著新的時刻加進來，實在不斷成長；這樣過去是固定的，未來是開放的。尷尬的問題是：你怎麼知道自己位於成長的那個邊緣？照這個看法，過去的人是真實的；他們也相信自己的那一刻是最新的，而他們錯了。

t.en: All times exist equally.
t.zh: 所有的時刻同樣存在。

r.en: This is the view most physicists find natural. Past and future are like distant places. You owe an account of why we experience a flow, why we fear future pain and feel only relief about past pain, and in what sense the future is open to choice if it is already there.
r.zh: 這是多數物理學家覺得自然的看法。過去與未來就像遙遠的地方。你欠一個說明：我們為什麼經驗到「流動」？我們為什麼害怕未來的痛苦，對過去的痛苦卻只感到鬆一口氣？還有，如果未來已經在那裡了，它在什麼意義上對選擇是開放的？

t.en: Time is not ultimately real.
t.zh: 時間終究不是真實的。

r.en: McTaggart argued that the idea of time is contradictory, and Nāgārjuna that past, present, and future cannot be established either together or apart. You must then explain what the appearance of time is an appearance of. Nāgārjuna has an answer that McTaggart lacks: conventional reality is real enough to live in, and its being conventional is what he calls its emptiness.
r.zh: 麥塔加論證「時間」這個觀念是自相矛盾的；龍樹論證過去、現在、未來不管合起來還是分開來，都無法成立。那麼你必須解釋：時間的表象，是什麼東西的表象？龍樹有一個麥塔加沒有的答案：世俗的實在，真實到足以讓人在其中生活；而它之為世俗，就是他所說的「空」。

argument.lead_en: McTaggart’s argument of 1908 concludes that time does not exist. Almost nobody accepts the conclusion, and every theory of time since has been built by rejecting one of his premises. Click a step to see what can be said against it.
argument.lead_zh: 麥塔加 1908 年的論證，結論是時間不存在。幾乎沒有人接受這個結論；而此後的每一個時間理論，都是靠否定他的某一個前提建立起來的。點任何一步，看看別人可以怎麼反對它。

steps.en: There is no time without change.
steps.zh: 沒有變化，就沒有時間。
steps.ob_en: Aristotle agreed, and Newton did not. Newton held that time would pass in a universe where nothing happened. It is not clear how anyone could tell.
steps.ob_zh: 亞里斯多德同意，牛頓不同意。牛頓主張，即使在一個什麼都沒發生的宇宙裡，時間也會流逝。至於誰能分辨得出來，並不清楚。

steps.en: Real change requires that events be first future, then present, then past. The fixed relations of earlier and later contain no change.
steps.zh: 真正的變化，需要事件先是未來的，然後是現在的，然後是過去的。「早於」與「晚於」這些固定的關係裡，並不包含變化。
steps.ob_en: This is the step most often attacked. Eternalists reply that change is simply a thing’s having different properties at different times: the poker is hot at noon and cold at midnight. No moving present is needed. McTaggart’s answer was that the poker’s being hot at noon is a fact that never alters, so nothing has really changed.
steps.ob_zh: 這是最常被攻擊的一步。永恆論者回答：變化不過是一樣東西在不同的時刻具有不同的性質：火鉗中午是熱的，午夜是冷的。不需要一個移動的「現在」。麥塔加的回應是：「火鉗在中午是熱的」是一個永遠不會改變的事實，所以其實沒有任何東西改變了。

steps.en: But past, present, and future are incompatible, and every event has all three.
steps.zh: 可是過去、現在、未來是互不相容的，而每一個事件三者都有。
steps.ob_en: The natural reply is that no event has them at once. It is future, then present, then past. McTaggart answered that “then” brings in time again, so that the explanation assumes what it was meant to explain, and a regress begins. Presentists reply that the regress is harmless, because only the present attributions are ever true.
steps.ob_zh: 很自然的回應是：沒有哪個事件是同時具有這三者的。它先是未來的，然後是現在的，然後是過去的。麥塔加回答：這個「然後」又把時間帶了進來；於是這個解釋預設了它本來要解釋的東西，一個後退就此開始。現在論者回答說，這個後退是無害的，因為只有「現在」的那些歸屬才為真。

steps.en: Therefore the moving present is contradictory, and since time requires it, time is unreal.
steps.zh: 所以，移動的「現在」是自相矛盾的；而既然時間需要它，時間就不是真實的。
steps.ob_en: Deny the second premise and you are an eternalist: time is real and does not flow. Deny the third and you are a presentist: time flows and only the present is real. The argument works as a fork in the road, and it is seldom treated as a proof.
steps.ob_zh: 否定第二個前提，你就是永恆論者：時間是真實的，但不流動。否定第三個前提，你就是現在論者：時間在流動，而只有現在是真實的。這個論證的作用像一個岔路口；很少有人把它當成一個證明。

source.work: Augustine, Confessions, Book XI
source.work_zh: 奧古斯丁《懺悔錄》卷十一
source.tr: translated by E. B. Pusey (public domain)
source.lead_en: Book XI is a commentary on the first words of Genesis, “In the beginning.” Augustine wants to know what it means for God to have made time, and the inquiry turns into the first sustained philosophy of time in the West. Pusey’s Victorian English keeps “thee” and “hath.”
source.lead_zh: 卷十一是對〈創世記〉開頭「起初」二字的註解。奧古斯丁想知道「上帝造了時間」是什麼意思，而這場探究成了西方第一部一氣呵成的時間哲學。Pusey 維多利亞時代的英譯保留了 thee、hath 這類古體。

passages.en: What then is time? If no one asks me, I know: if I wish to explain it to one that asketh, I know not: yet I say boldly that I know, that if nothing passed away, time past were not; and if nothing were coming, a time to come were not; and if nothing were, time present were not.
passages.zh: 那麼時間是什麼？沒有人問我，我是知道的；如果我想向發問的人解釋，我就不知道了。但我敢大膽地說，我知道：如果沒有東西過去，就沒有過去的時間；如果沒有東西到來，就沒有將來的時間；如果沒有東西存在，就沒有現在的時間。
passages.note_en: The famous confession of ignorance is only the first half of the sentence. Read the second half. He does know something, and says so “boldly”: time depends on things passing away, coming, and being. That is Aristotle’s position, that there is no time without change, and it is the first premise of McTaggart’s argument. The humility is real, and it is also a method. He separates the little that he can assert from the much that he cannot. (“Were not” is the old form of “would not be.”)
passages.note_zh: 那句著名的「承認無知」，只是這個句子的前半。讀讀後半。他確實知道一些東西，而且說自己是「大膽地」說：時間取決於事物的過去、到來與存在。這就是亞里斯多德的立場——沒有變化就沒有時間——也是麥塔加論證的第一個前提。這份謙遜是真的，同時也是一種方法。他把自己能斷言的那一點點，跟不能斷言的一大片分開。（were not 是 would not be 的古體。）

passages.en: …yet perchance it might be properly said, “there be three times; a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future.” For these three do exist in some sort, in the soul, but otherwhere do I not see them; present of things past, memory; present of things present, sight; present of things future, expectation.
passages.zh: ……不過，這樣說或許才恰當：「時間有三種：過去事物的現在、現在事物的現在、未來事物的現在。」因為這三者確實以某種方式存在於靈魂之中，在別處我看不到它們：過去事物的現在是記憶；現在事物的現在是直觀；未來事物的現在是期待。
passages.note_en: Look at the qualifications: “perchance,” “in some sort,” “otherwhere do I not see them.” He is reporting where he can find past and future, and he does not claim that they exist nowhere else. The move is to turn a question about the world into a question about experience, and it was made again fifteen centuries later by Husserl, who analyzed the experience of hearing a melody in almost the same three terms. (“Perchance” means “perhaps,” and “otherwhere” means “elsewhere.”)
passages.note_zh: 看看那些限定語：「或許」「以某種方式」「在別處我看不到它們」。他報告的是他在哪裡「找得到」過去與未來，並沒有宣稱它們在別處都不存在。這一步，是把一個關於世界的問題，轉成一個關於經驗的問題；一千五百年後，胡塞爾又走了一次這一步，他用幾乎相同的三個項目，分析了「聽一段旋律」的經驗。（perchance 是「或許」，otherwhere 是「別處」。）

items.o_en: Augustine makes time depend on the mind. But the dinosaurs lived and died over a hundred million years with no one to remember or expect anything.
items.o_zh: 奧古斯丁讓時間依賴於心靈。可是恐龍活了又死了一億多年，當時並沒有任何人在記憶或期待什麼。
items.r_en: The objection is sound against the claim that there was no time before minds, and he does not make that claim. He holds that time began with the created world. What he places in the mind is our measuring of time and the three tenses. A modern eternalist can agree with him exactly: the order of earlier and later is in the world, and pastness, presentness, and futurity come from the standpoint of an experiencer.
items.r_zh: 如果針對的是「在有心靈之前沒有時間」這個主張，這個反駁是成立的；但他並沒有這樣主張。他認為時間是跟受造的世界一起開始的。他放進心靈裡的，是我們對時間的度量，以及三種時態。現代的永恆論者可以跟他完全一致：「早於」與「晚於」的次序在世界裡；而「過去」「現在」「未來」這些性質，來自經驗者的立足點。

items.o_en: Physics has settled the matter. Relativity shows that there is no universal present, so the flow of time is an illusion and philosophers have nothing to add.
items.o_zh: 物理學已經解決了這件事。相對論顯示沒有普遍的現在，所以時間的流動是幻覺，哲學家沒有什麼可補充的。
items.r_en: Relativity rules out a universal present defined by physics. It does not rule out a privileged present that physics cannot detect, though few find that attractive. More to the point, calling the flow an illusion does not explain it. An illusion is an experience, and an experience of passage seems itself to be something that passes. Explaining how a world without passage produces minds for which there is passage is unfinished work in physics and philosophy alike.
items.r_zh: 相對論排除的是「由物理學界定的普遍現在」。它並沒有排除一個物理學偵測不到的、享有特殊地位的現在，雖然很少有人覺得那有吸引力。更要緊的是：把流動稱為幻覺，並沒有解釋它。幻覺是一種經驗；而一個「流逝」的經驗，本身似乎就是某種在流逝的東西。解釋一個沒有流逝的世界，怎麼產生出「對它們而言有流逝」的心靈，這在物理學與哲學裡同樣是未完成的工作。

items.o_en: The question is empty. Time is what clocks measure, and nothing more needs to be said.
items.o_zh: 這個問題是空的。時間就是時鐘量出來的東西，沒有別的需要說。
items.r_en: This is a good definition for doing physics, and it leaves the philosophical question where it was. A clock is a process that repeats, and to call it a good clock is to say that its repetitions take equal times, which uses the idea we were trying to define. The definition also says nothing about the difference between past and future, since a clock runs equally well in a film played backward.
items.r_zh: 對於做物理學，這是個好定義；而它讓哲學問題留在原地。時鐘是一個會重複的過程；說它是一個好時鐘，就是說它每一次重複所花的時間相等，而這用到了我們正要定義的那個觀念。這個定義對過去與未來的差別也什麼都沒說，因為在倒著播放的影片裡，時鐘走得同樣順暢。

said.claim: Asked what God was doing before he made the world, Augustine replied: “Preparing hell for people who ask such questions.”
said.claim_zh: 有人問上帝在創造世界之前做什麼，奧古斯丁回答：「在為問這種問題的人準備地獄。」
said.verdict_en: He quotes it to reject it
said.verdict_zh: 他引這句話，是為了拒絕它
said.en: The joke is in the Confessions, and Augustine says plainly that he will not use it. “I answer not as one is said to have done merrily … ‘He was preparing hell (saith he) for pryers into mysteries.’ It is one thing to answer enquiries, another to make sport of enquirers.” His own answer is philosophical: there was no “before,” because time was created with the world. “There was no ‘then,’ when there was no time.”
said.zh: 這個笑話確實在《懺悔錄》裡，而奧古斯丁明白地說他不會用它。「我不像據說有人戲謔地回答的那樣……『他在為窺探奧祕的人準備地獄。』回答提問是一回事，取笑提問的人是另一回事。」他自己的回答是哲學的：根本沒有「之前」，因為時間是跟世界一起被造的。「沒有時間的時候，就沒有『那時』。」

terms.d_en: The view that only present things exist.
terms.d_zh: 主張只有現在的事物存在。
